newsitem.title: USA: IMM currency futures finish on a weak note.
newsitem.headline: IMM currency futures finish on a weak note.

text.p: Most IMM currency futures ended on a weak note, as the U.S. dollar held its gains despite several bouts of profit-taking, traders said.

Yen futures erased the day's gains at midsession after Iraq said it fired three missiles at U.S. planes. Dealers were aggressive sellers, traders said. Dealers continued to press December to $0.009183, despite one bank's buying 500 contracts at $0.009185.
Analysts said the technical failure of dollar/yen to puncture the 109.89 level led to a dealer attempt to drive the dollar/yen to the upside.

Earlier one bank sold December yen at $0.009205 when the dollar/yen rate fell to 110.05 spot. But late in the day as the dollar/yen was probing 110.20, one U.S. institution sold 500 December yen at $0.009189 in the all-or-nothing pit.
"There is now the sense that the dollar/yen will test the 110.50 level," one floor trader said. "But who knows how many exporter orders are at that level."
The 110.50 spot level corresponds to $0.009169, which is below the December yen's contract low at $0.009183.
Rob Fullem, a currency analyst at NatWest Markets, said the dollar is technically due for a pullback in the near term.
"The dollar has come a long way," Fullem said. "People are a little too euphoric on the dollar."
December marks briefly dipped to $0.6638 on lingering concerns about Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher's comments overnight. He said German interest rates could fall further.

The comments contributed to suspicions circulating on the floor of the IMM and in forex trading rooms that the Swiss National Bank was injecting liquidity into the markets, thereby keeping both December marks and Swiss francs pinned to the downside.

"The key factors driving the dollar higher have been central bank dollar-buying, the Bundesbank easing the repo rate and the SNB's continual policy of easing," Fullem said. "This smacks of coordinated central bank intervention."
"They intervene in a subtle way, but regardless, they are still intervening," he added.

Several analysts said they were tracking the amount of dollars purchased by central banks, as participation by foreign central banks has increased since the last two weeks of August. December marks appeared to find some relief from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer's comments, they said.
Tietmeyer said the EMU candidates must prove they can keep lasting fiscal discipline and that the core EMU was possible if Germany and France continued their current policies.

At the end of pit trade, December yen fell $0.000006 at $0.009190, marks were off $0.0017 at $0.6650, Swiss francs off $0.0027 at $0.8148, sterling off $0.0014 at $1.5538, Canadian dollars were off $0.0001 at $0.7320 and Australian dollars were down $0.0027 at $0.7944.
